lead: A fire protection system watches the engines, APU, cargo holds and lavatories for heat, flame or smoke, raises a cockpit warning, and lets the crew, or an automatic circuit, release a stored extinguishing agent into the affected zone. It exists because a fire in a hidden compartment can grow faster than anyone can see it. Fast detection, very few false alarms and a reliable discharge path are the design aims.
prereq: You need the engine and APU zone layout from engine fuel and lubricating systems, and circuit protection from the aircraft electrical systems topic.

blocks.text: Fire protection has two separate jobs. Detection watches a zone and decides that a fire exists. Extinguishing carries agent to that zone. The two jobs meet at the control unit and the cockpit. A smoke detector in a cargo hold does not put out a fire; it only starts the warning chain.

items: Fast response: the detector must signal within seconds of a flame or a temperature rise, before the fire spreads.
Low false alarms: a warning that cries wolf makes the crew ignore a real fire. The control unit uses a short confirmation delay and compares more than one sensor where possible.
Full zone coverage: no shadow area. A continuous loop or several spot detectors are placed so that any fire in the zone heats at least one sensor.
Testable and resettable: a test switch simulates a detector. After the test the system must return to normal without replacing parts.
Fault indication: a broken wire or a failed detector must show as a fault, not as a healthy zone or as a fire.
Survive the environment: vibration, heat, fuel, oil and cleaning fluids.

blocks.text: The detector is chosen for the zone. An engine nacelle has airflow and hot metal; a cargo hold has boxes and possible smouldering. One detector type does not fit all.

items: Thermocouple: several active junctions in the zone are wired against reference junctions kept cool. A fast temperature rise makes a voltage that trips a sensitive relay, so it detects the rate of rise, not a fixed temperature.
Bimetallic spot detector: two metals with different expansion bend a strip; at a set temperature it closes a contact. It protects one small point.

Continuous loop (resistance type): an Inconel tube with one centre wire (Fenwal) or two wires (Kidde) is packed with a eutectic salt or thermistor material whose resistance falls sharply when hot. A low resistance anywhere along the loop gives a warning.

Continuous loop (pneumatic type): a sealed tube holds a gas and a gas-charged core (the Lindberg or Systron-Donner type). Heat raises the pressure and closes a diaphragm switch: a general overheat raises the gas pressure, a local fire releases gas from the core.
Flame detectors: ultraviolet or infrared cells see the light of a flame within a second; they are paired or filtered so sunlight does not trip them.

Smoke detectors: an ionisation detector loses current when smoke enters its chamber; an optical detector sees light scattered by smoke onto a photocell. Both suit cargo holds and lavatories, where smoke arrives before flame.
Carbon monoxide detector: an electrochemical cell catches a slow, smouldering fire that makes little visible smoke.

blocks.text: The control unit supplies power, watches the loops and decides. It applies a short delay to reject a transient, drives the warning light and bell, and stores a fault code. The test switch injects a simulated detector signal. Crews test the loops before flight; the system then resets.

Engine and APU zones usually have two identical loops, A and B, in AND logic: both must sense a fire before the warning shows, which stops a damaged loop giving a false alarm. If one loop fails, the control unit shows a FAULT and switches to the healthy loop alone, so a single broken wire does not lose protection.

When the control unit confirms a fire, the cockpit gets a red fire light and a bell. On many types the pilot then pulls the fire handle: pulling closes the fuel (spar) valve, the hydraulic shut-off valve and the bleed valve, trips the generator and arms the squib circuit; rotating the handle then fires a squib. Other types use a guarded fire push-button and separate agent buttons. On the ground an APU fire usually shuts the APU down and fires its bottle automatically; in flight the crew uses the APU fire control.

A squib is a small explosive cartridge. It drives a cutter or opens the bottle valve. One squib gives one shot; after firing it is spent. Some installations carry two bottles, or a bottle with two squibs, so the crew can fire a second shot after the first has knocked the fire down.

Engine and APU bottles sit outside the fire zone: the APU bottle in the tail cone or aft bay, the engine bottles in the pylon, wing root or fuselage, with pipes to nozzles in the nacelle. Cargo holds are classed by how a fire is handled: in a Class C hold (the usual lower-deck hold) there are smoke detectors and a built-in extinguishing system, fired from the cockpit with a first high-rate discharge and then a metered flow that holds the concentration until landing; a Class E hold on a freighter has detection, and the crew shuts off the airflow to starve the fire. A lavatory waste bin has a small bottle with a fusible link that discharges by itself. Portable extinguishers in the cabin are for the crew.

The agent volume follows V<sub>a</sub> = C × V<sub>z</sub> ÷ (1 − C), where V<sub>a</sub> is the volume of agent vapour needed in m³, C is the design concentration as a fraction and V<sub>z</sub> is the zone volume in m³. The division by (1 − C) allows for the air the agent pushes out. The mass is m = V<sub>a</sub> × ρ, with ρ the agent vapour density.

Halon 1301 is a clean agent: it leaves no residue and breaks the chemical chain of combustion, so a few per cent stops a flame. It depletes ozone, so it is no longer made and aviation uses recycled stock while replacements are approved. Carbon dioxide is not used in occupied spaces because it can suffocate; water and dry powder suit hand-held cabin use.

spec.aria: An engine nacelle with two detector loops A and B feeding a control unit with AND logic, which lights the fire light and bell; the pilot pulls then turns the fire handle, a squib fires and the bottle sends agent back to the nacelle. A note says a failed loop gives a fault and the other works alone. Bottom box: a 40 cubic metre hold at 6 percent needs 2.55 cubic metres, 15.3 kilograms.

examples.question: A cargo compartment has a volume of 40 m³. The design agent concentration is 6 % by volume and the agent vapour density is 6 kg/m³. Find the agent vapour volume and mass, and the error if the simple form V<sub>a</sub> = C × V<sub>z</sub> is used.
steps: Agent volume: V<sub>a</sub> = C × V<sub>z</sub> ÷ (1 − C) = 0.06 × 40 ÷ 0.94 = 2.553 m³.
Agent mass: m = V<sub>a</sub> × ρ = 2.553 × 6 = 15.3 kg.
Difference: 15.3 − 14.4 = 0.9 kg, the simple form is 6 % low (1 − 0.94).
examples.answer: About 2.55 m³ of agent vapour, 15.3 kg of agent stored as liquid in the bottle; the simple form would give only 14.4 kg.

traps: Smoke detection is not suppression. A cargo smoke warning starts the chain; the bottles do the extinguishing.
On fire-handle types the handle has two actions: pulling isolates and arms, rotating discharges. Writing only "pull to discharge" loses marks.
A squib is one-shot. A test does not fire the squib; it only tests the circuit.
Halon 1301 does not work mainly by removing oxygen. It breaks the chemical chain, so a low concentration can stop a flame.

Dual loops in AND logic need both loops to warn; that cuts false alarms, and a failed loop is dropped automatically with a FAULT light, so writing "one loop must fail before the other works" is wrong.

quiz.q: Name four zones protected by fire detection on a typical transport aircraft.
quiz.a: Engine, APU, cargo compartment and lavatory; many types also monitor the wheel well and the avionics bay.

quiz.q: Why does a continuous loop cover a zone better than a single spot detector?
quiz.a: The tube runs around the whole zone. Any local heat changes the loop and is sensed, so there is no shadow area. A spot detector sees only its own small point.

quiz.q: A cargo hold of 30 m³ needs 5 % agent by volume. The agent vapour density is 6 kg/m³. Find the agent mass.
A cargo smoke detector alarms, but no fire is found. Give two design features that reduce such false alarms and explain each.
quiz.a: A short confirmation delay rejects a transient such as dust or steam. AND logic between two detectors or loops needs two sensors to agree before the warning, so one faulty sensor cannot start the discharge chain.
It is a small explosive cartridge that opens the bottle valve or drives a cutter when fired.

quiz.q: Why is carbon dioxide not used in an occupied cabin?
quiz.a: It displaces oxygen and can suffocate people. It is suitable for an unoccupied compartment, not a cabin with crew or passengers.

quiz.q: The fire handle is pulled but not rotated. Does agent discharge? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Pulling isolates the fuel, hydraulic and bleed supplies and arms the squib circuit. Rotating the handle is the action that fires the squib and discharges the agent.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer cargo holds use fibre-optic linear heat sensing and video smoke detection to cut false alarms. Halon replacements for engine nacelles and cargo holds are still being certified. Search for "aircraft cargo fire suppression", "Halon 1301 replacement" and "continuous loop fire detector".
